entry.summary: HORIZON3 Modern hacking rarely happens the way you expect, so in late 2026 Horizon3 kicked off The Attack Path Tour, a series of live events, across several cities in the US, to share insights, technical deep dives and discussions surrounding the topic with fellow security practi
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Abraham E. • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d, Motion Design, BTS

HORIZON3

Modern hacking rarely happens the way you expect, so in late 2026 Horizon3 kicked off The Attack Path Tour, a series of live events, across several cities in the US, to share insights, technical deep dives and discussions surrounding the topic with fellow security practitioners.

For their inaugural series, they reached out to Buff to craft a high-energy, 2D opener to build anticipation and excitement for audiences before keynote talks began, and I had the opportunity to bring the opener to life w/ the Buff crew.

Double-check your passwords, dim your lights and enjoy:

In cyber security, attack paths are the chain of small, but connected vulnerabilities a hacker strings together to reach into a larger system, akin to how a thief might break into your home through unlocked doors, eventually reaching for your precious collection of Funko POPs .

NodeZero, Horizon3's AI hacker, runs automated penetration tests (Pentests), to test these vulnerabilities and generate a report, so you know exactly how it got in and patch recommendations, so you stay out of the news :)

As we learnt more about the product, pentesting and attack paths, I sketched, revised, laughed, loved, and fed back with the team, refining very rough storyboards of key ideas and features that made NodeZero stand out;
​​​​​​​

These were then vectorised as storyboards, shared early on w/ the client, fedback and inevitably iterated on further to accommodate the clients needs, eventually leading to the final* greyscale storyboards below:

At the time, Horizon3’s visual identity was still developing, especially for animation, where we wanted to really create something different and bold.

We knew we wanted to keep things mostly 2D, both for familiarity and efficiency, but also needed to explore some of our early ideas, like conveying the overwhelming speed of NodeZero’s probing, how colour and light might behave during breaches, and stylised attack paths. Below are some of the early designs I developed alongside the wonderful Margo Semcuk in Figma.

With the above (eventually) approved by the client, I armed myself with more references, some fruit and a banging music playlist, as I then translated all the earlier greyscale storyboards into the final-look frames below, with great feedback from Margo along the way; playing with gradients, light and close-ups for added drama

The design organically became more nuanced, and gradients, glows and 3D elements (even if faux) became quite time-consuming to add in animation. While we wish we had more time to add all the subtle details we envisioned (and more), making sure the most important things were well animated and shaded became the priority ahead of the deadline.

Glossy gradient orbs, 3D icons and a whole lot of (hand-animated) particles and trails were explored in this one, with some lil tricks I managed to develop (and rediscover) along the way. Pick your fave:)

- First things first: Focus on the primary elements first, both in design and animation, and really nail those. Secondary elements can’t fix an ugly design/animation.

- Do the best you can: Being responsible for storyboards and final-look styleframes was admittedly daunting, but the visual approach and creative freedom made the challenge all the more feasible. I am capable, and just had to try my best here.

- Yes and: Sometimes client notes can really throw off your vision, but try understanding what the real issue is, and coming up with a beautiful solution, if possible :)

- Always CC: No matter how flat, always add some colour corrections to the final render, especially if there’s gradients. Treat colour correction as part of the animation, not an optional afterthought.

entry.content:
▶ Ver y reproducir video en FrameRate (0:20)

Estudio / Creador: Bishnu Kumar

A 20-second social ad, designed and animated in one week.

Everyday drinks reveal how much water shapes flavour, leading to one simple message: not all water is created equal.

The moodboard established a clean, graphic direction built around fluid forms, everyday drinking moments, and Cedar Springs’ darker brand palette.

I planned the sequence around the voiceover: glass and ice, coffee and tea, then a droplet leading into the Cedar Springs bottle.

Simple vector shapes established consistent proportions and perspective across the glass, cup, and bottle.

The key style frames establish the darker visual direction across the glass, tea, pour, and Cedar Springs bottle.

The cup and glass were built in Illustrator and transferred to After Effects with Overlord. I hand-keyframed the liquid, a “poor man’s fluid simulation.” The toughest part was making the ice feel buoyant as it dropped into the water and gradually slowed down. It was more complex than expected, and I learned a lot from it.

Six motion studies, including ice built with After Effects’ 3D tools.

Animation followed the ElevenLabs voiceover. After picture lock, I layered glass, ice, liquid sounds, and transition accents over music licensed through Motion Array.

Matthew Corrales, Teaching Assistant at School of Motion, praised the film’s simplicity and flow. His notes focused on smoother coffee-to-tea transitions, tighter match cuts between cups, and a more seamless move into the overhead shot.

“Very clean design that says a lot without needing to show a lot.”

— MATTHEW CORRALES, TEACHING ASSISTANT, SCHOOL OF MOTION

Delivered in one week for sponsored Facebook and Instagram advertising across the Greater Toronto Area. The client said the film exceeded their expectations.

But also do it so it's damn sexy, and allows us to play with 3D.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Jacob How • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 3d

SIX AUDIO-REACTIVE 3D ANIMATIONS

I built six visual systems from six tracks. Each study starts with colors drawn from its record or single artwork, then uses repetition and depth to give the sound a distinct setting.

In ten, the floral shape sits inside a tight radial field. In Apricots, I move from a single coral form to a dense field of repeated marks. In Angels, softer lavender and sage and more space between forms give the sequence a pause.

Like A Fool starts with a bright checkerboard and pale floral shapes. I used repeated cylinders and a blue tunnel to carry the pattern into depth. The two frames show how a repeated form can behave like a graphic surface in one shot and a space the camera can move through in the next.

03:00 Apricots — BICEP

entry.summary: INDEPENDENT VISUAL ALBUM REWORK I animated all eleven tracks of Jamie xx’s debut album as an independent visual rework. Over 42 minutes and 45 seconds, each chapter gives the music its own movement and carries one color into the next. Rose Pilkington’s visual work for Jamie xx le
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Jacob How • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 3d

INDEPENDENT VISUAL ALBUM REWORK

I animated all eleven tracks of Jamie xx’s debut album as an independent visual rework. Over 42 minutes and 45 seconds, each chapter gives the music its own movement and carries one color into the next.

Rose Pilkington’s visual work for Jamie xx led me to Cinema 4D. I took on the full album as a self-directed way to learn the software and answer a design question: how do eleven animations feel related when the songs move at different speeds and carry different emotions? I restricted every chapter to a palette of five colors or fewer. Across the cuts I let one color survive, so a change in energy or density still feels like part of the same film.

I listened for changes in pace, energy and structure before building a scene. I set out rectangles, planes and triangles, then tested which part of the sound should change scale, rotation, visibility or timing. Sleep Sound needed room for slowly shifting vertical forms. Obvs needed pieces that could separate and reassemble. I used MoGraph Cloners, Effectors, Fields and Fracture for those different kinds of movement, then adjusted materials and camera timing by hand. I rebuilt scenes as I learned which decisions needed direct control.

01 Gosh · 02 Sleep Sound · 03 SeeSaw · 04 Obvs · 05 Just Saying · 06 Stranger in a Room · 07 Hold Tight · 08 Loud Places · 09 I Know There’s Gonna Be (Good Times) · 10 The Rest Is Noise · 11 Girl

Music: Jamie xx, In Colour (2015). SeeSaw and Loud Places feature Romy, Stranger in a Room features Oliver Sim, and I Know There’s Gonna Be (Good Times) features Young Thug and Popcaan. Visual direction, design and animation: Jacob How. An independent visual rework.

Gosh builds architectural mass through slow reveals as the music gathers. In Sleep Sound, violet columns drift and regroup in a blue space. SeeSaw uses offset planes and a shifting viewpoint to keep the composition from settling. In Obvs, the recurring motion is a cycle of fragments separating and locking back together. In each case I could keep the same basic vocabulary of shapes and change their behavior.

Just Saying pulls the motion into a compact radial space so the pulse stays legible. Stranger in a Room thins the scene and lets isolated forms disappear into negative space. In Hold Tight, hard yellow crossings build tension through overlap. Loud Places gives the frame more layers as the arrangement opens up. The changes in density are part of the pacing of the album.

Good Times puts bright geometric fragments in rapid motion. The Rest Is Noise gives abstract color and form room to build before the closing chapter. Girl brings fractured shapes and multiple colors back into the same frame. I approached the ending as a return to the vocabulary of the album, with more of the palette visible at once.

Across 153,915 frames, I returned to the same design problem at different speeds and scales. The long format made it clear when a camera move was doing more work than the geometry, or when a transition needed a held color more than another effect. The result is a collection of distinct chapters and a record of how I learned to direct procedural motion over the length of an album. I brought the same attention to pacing and recurring forms into my own music for Violet Spiral.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Jacob How • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 3d

AUDIOVISUAL ALBUM

I compose electronic music and build a 3D animation system for each track. Violet connects the films while each track develops its own palette and rhythm.

A rosette gives the films a common starting point. Arrival begins with a blue rosette on red and ends in a warm field of dots. Within Reach moves from orange and green into magenta beams and violet forms. Starlight tilts a yellow lattice into cyan and green. Open Circuit puts magenta against chartreuse and teal. Luminance moves from a blue rosette on green to dark violet and a final burst of pale rays.

I compose and arrange in Logic Pro. In Cinema 4D, separate Sound Effectors let individual parts of the mix drive different changes in the geometry. In Starlight, sustained strings and short percussion events feed separate inputs. Cloners and Delay build the repetition, while camera and material keyframes shape the change from closed grids to long streaks.

Music, production, mixing, direction, 3D animation and artwork by Jacob How. Watch the five released films below in release order.

entry.summary: Time to boogie. An unreleased robot, brought back to life. raven R (only R after this) is a speaker-robot concept designed by Teenage Engineering that never made it to market. I've always felt it deserved better than a shelf in the archive, so I decided to bring it back from the
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Peter Pongó • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 3d, Motion Design, Short Film

Time to boogie.

An unreleased robot, brought back to life. raven R (only R after this) is a speaker-robot concept designed by Teenage Engineering that never made it to market. I've always felt it deserved better than a shelf in the archive, so I decided to bring it back from the grave (and make a cool project out of it).

Product doesn't have to be released to be loved. I wanted to show how a R can play on people's feelings: how movement, rhythm and sound can make a audience care about something that is, on paper, just a machine. R is the perfect subject because it doesn't just play music, it is supposed to perform it.

The music choice came first right on the beginning of the project, without it I wouldn't even start. R is very expressive in the way it moves, and I wanted a track with the same personality: warm, a little melancholic, playful and full of feeling. “Heartaches” by The Marcels has all of that. These days, there’s a growing disconnect between humans and robots. We tend to see them as a threat, something built to take our jobs. But not every robot is here to replace us. Some are here simply to make us feel more whole. With R, my goal was to bridge that gap and connect people with robots through music.

The teaser started as part of the main video, but I later separated it into its own piece. It presents Raven R as a mystery to be unraveled: first in the dark, where the viewer only catches hints of what’s there. Then comes the second reveal, a total switch to a whimsical, dancing robot.

Before any animation was made, I built a storyboard to get the mental image out of my head in Figma. The goal was to confirm the concept worked before investing time in the production: that the story reads clearly, the pacing supports the music, and each part carries the emotion I was after.

ADDITIONAL CONTENT

Posters

Alongside the main film, R will get a series of short videos made for socials. Each one is a small moment that lets the viewer connect with the robot through movement and music, and each uses a different genre to reach even wider audience. They’re still in development and will be released down the line.

R was produced entirely in Blender. Working solo, I handled every step of the pipeline myself, from the storyboard to the final edit and sound design. That gave me full control over the result: the movement of the robot, the timing against the music and the mood of each scene all come from the same hands.

R needed to look and feel like a real, physical product, so I spent a lot of time on the materials. To make it dance, I built a rig that gives it expressive, flexible movement while staying true to how a small robot like this would move. A good rig lets me animate with personality, so every bounce, tilt and head movement is timed to the music and reads as emotion, not just motion.

I work with studios and agencies on product films, campaigns and short-form content. Let’s make something people feel: hi@peterpongo.com

entry.summary: BLINK · 2026 A launch film for Blinkids: savings and investment accounts that parents open for their children. Client: Blink (heyblink.com) Year: 2026 Role: Creative Director, Design & Animation Field: Motion design Blink is an investment app. But that description undersells the
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Guy Nativ • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 2d

BLINK · 2026

A launch film for Blinkids: savings and investment accounts that parents open for their children.

Client: Blink (heyblink.com) Year: 2026 Role: Creative Director, Design & Animation Field: Motion design

Blink is an investment app. But that description undersells the idea behind it. Blink is built around a life cycle. Your parents open an account for you as a kid. You grow up with it. Then one day you open one for your own kids. It’s meant to stay with you for life. Blinkids is their new feature: savings and investment accounts that parents open for their children. This film was made to launch it. The goal: make investing for your kids feel simple.

Most investment apps look the same. Dense graphs, blinking numbers, screens built for traders. That look doesn’t work when you’re asking a parent to think about their child’s future.

The challenge: make investing for your kids feel simple and warm, not intimidating. And communicate the life cycle idea, that Blink is more than an app, it’s something that follows you through life, in about a minute.

I got the project with a script only. No boards, no design, no visual direction.

The first thing I did was edit the script. Before touching a single frame, the story had to be tight. I cut what didn’t serve the launch and sharpened what did.

Then came the rough storyboard. This is where the real decisions happen. It’s fast, it’s sketchy, and that’s the point. Shai Lanir, Blink’s Head of Design, and I went back and forth here. Real conversation, real notes, real precision. Changes at this stage cost minutes, not days.

Only after the storyboard was locked did design begin. That’s how I always work. Before the animation starts, the design has to work.

The easy choice was to look like every other finance app. Dark UI, glowing graphs, serious tone. We went the other way.

Simple shapes. Bold, warm colors. Yellow, pink, purple, teal, deep navy. Flat illustration with strong shadows. Real photos of real people inside the UI, so the product feels human, not hypothetical.

When the film talks about investing, the visuals show coffee and cookies next to the graph. That was the whole point: investing for your kids should feel as casual as your morning coffee, not like a trading floor.

Every screen in the film shows a real moment in the product: opening a plan for your kid, naming it, watching it grow over time. And in key moments, like setting the amount or the deposit date, we simplified the UI even further. Fewer elements, more air. The simplicity isn’t claimed, it’s shown.

Typography carries the story between scenes, big and confident, never crowded.

The result is a film about money that doesn’t feel like a film about money. It feels like a film about family.

Client Feedback

“As a designer, I can’t help the urge to try and control every tiny detail. But I also know my limits, and the only way to create something truly great is by joining forces with other super talented people. Guy is exactly that. He completely got the vibe, and gave it motion without losing what made it feel like Blink. And then he brought in Tal Avital to take it one step further with tailored sound design, which really made the whole thing pop. Super happy with how this turned out. Great people, great process, great result.”

— Shai Lanir, Head of Design, Blink

“Hey Guy, it came out stunning!”

— Shlomit, Co-CEO & Co-Founder, Blink

ALTA AI · 2025

A 30-second product film for Katie, Alta’s AI SDR agent.

Client: Alta (altahq.com) Year: 2025 Role: Animator Field: Motion design

Alta builds AI-powered agents that help sales teams work smarter. Katie is their SDR agent, the one that takes action so your team doesn’t have to. The goal was to make that feel real in 30 seconds.

We opened with chaos. An overwhelming calendar, too many tasks, no clear path. Then Katie enters, and suddenly everything clicks into place.

The contrast was intentional. Chaos first, clarity after. That’s what Katie does.

30 seconds is short. Every frame had to earn its place.

Some beautifully animated scenes didn’t make the cut because they didn’t serve the bigger picture.

entry.title: It's so lonely out here. – thijs merckx
entry.summary: PERSONAL PROJECT A 28-second loop about the thing that links my experience of this year's total solar eclipse, Sputnik 1 and Voyager 1: a change in perspective, and the loneliness that comes with it. The scale of things in space messes with my head, and I love it when a fact mana
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: thijs merckx • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d

PERSONAL PROJECT

A 28-second loop about the thing that links my experience of this year's total solar eclipse, Sputnik 1 and Voyager 1: a change in perspective, and the loneliness that comes with it.

The scale of things in space messes with my head, and I love it when a fact manages to make it tangible. Funny, isn't it, that the Moon is about 400 times closer to us than the Sun, and just about as many times smaller? A coincidence that gives us total solar eclipses, like the beautiful one I watched from a mountaintop in Spain last summer.

Add Sputnik 1, the first thing we ever put in orbit, and Voyager 1, the farthest, which looked back at our Pale Blue Dot in 1990 (and is now about to be a full light-day away).

Three changes in perspective. Each a little lonelier than the last.

01 · REFERENCE: Notice, then simplify

I started from my own experience during the eclipse: the Sun's corona and the pure black disc at its centre. Then I went online looking for archive pictures of Sputnik and Voyager. I simplified it all to match the look of my new website. What's left is thin lines and one black shape that play nicely with 2D animation.

02 · LIGHT: Depth without 3D

To give every object its position in space, and to make one element transform smoothly into the next, I had to play with light. It's very effective at making a flat shape 'turn'. The trickiest bit was the shadows of Voyager's antenna struts inside its dish. They had to stick to the hexagon shadow the dish casts, while everything sat nested in one layer and the whole spacecraft rotated. Claude helped me write the expressions that create the links. They still drifted at the extremes, so I added a point control to steer the last bit by hand.

03 · ANIMATION: Incorrect, yet my own

Why go to all that trouble? The rig let me animate fluidly without worrying about the shadow, and it allowed me to break with realism: nudging the shadow by hand until the motion felt like mine.

04 · SOUND: Decompose, recompose

Sound isn't my field, so for this personal piece I turned to Claude. I wanted the sound to carry the contrast between the enormous Sun and its corona and the small, lonely spacecraft drifting past. My suggestion: a deep solar rumble, chimes for the eclipse, pure bleeps for the two spacecraft. Claude synthesised them from scratch. The results weren't all that great. The mixes were a bit 'much', distracting and often badly timed. So I asked for every sample as a separate file and did the timing, layering and effects myself.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Make Good Studio • Categoría: Animation

AN ORIGINAL MAKE GOOD FILM

Two small friends. One enormous shadow. An unexpected companion.

Lilac and Periwinkle take a lantern into the woods. Their shadow puppet game attracts a much bigger participant. The enormous shadow looks like trouble, until we meet the shaggy Bigfoot making it. When the light starts to leave, his confidence goes with it.

Make Good created this original studio concept for ROAM, a fictional LED lantern brand. The product starts the game, reveals the misunderstanding, and gives three unlikely friends a reason to walk home together.

The lantern combines a directional beam for shadow play with a broad glow for walking together. That change of light is also a change in the story: a source of playful scares becomes a small place of safety.

Early storyboards helped us test the reveal and the ending. Individual frames were then revised so the lantern stayed on the same rock, the hand pose matched its shadow, and the moon belonged to one sky rather than every camera angle.

Character sheets establish identity, storyboard frames establish composition, and the forest reference establishes materials and atmosphere. Giving each reference a clear job made individual performances easier to revise.

For the closing walk, a simple Blender guide moves the camera backward and slightly upward as the trio walks away. It supplies the trajectory, not the finished fur or faces. The selected generated take follows that move while giving each character a different walking rhythm.

Bigfoot needs to look imposing before he looks vulnerable. His hesitation at the dark path makes the invitation matter. Small reactions, offset gestures, and a close view between wider shots give the characters room to respond.

Consistency also lives in tiny details. Lilac and Periwinkle keep small dark eyes, while Bigfoot retains his larger eyes with visible whites. The final edit trims away camera glances and gestures that pull attention out of the story.

In DaVinci Resolve, narration, nonverbal reactions, selected generated scene sounds, and a subtle forest bed support the rhythm. The playful music carries the change in mood, and the final product hold gives the ending time to land.

Creative direction and production: Josh Good / Make Good Studio. Concept, character and product development, storyboards, AI production, camera blocking, editing and sound.

Music: “Sneaky Grandma” by The Fly Guy Five, sourced from Epidemic Sound. Still development used ChatGPT image generation; motion used MiniMax H3 Max through fal, with Blender camera guides. ElevenLabs supported narration and character vocal development. The film was edited in DaVinci Resolve.

ROAM is a fictional brand created for this original studio concept. Explore the full production story at https://makegood.tv/projects/roam-ai-character-animation.

entry.content:
▶ Ver y reproducir video en FrameRate (1:38)

Estudio / Creador: Yassine Khiari • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d, 3d, Hand Drawn

As we dive within the meanings hidden between the lines and the feelings expressed in the poem, an illustrated animation unveils as we accompany the olives in an exciting adventure through their lifetime from birth, growing up in a family while facing the elements of nature, seeing the process of oil production from their point of view, until they reach their ultimate transformation in the form of the glorious golden olive oil. The journey comes to an end as the oil rests inside our product’s bottle: Their new home.

A Touching Poem Begging to Be Visualized!

I was tremendously excited when I first heard the Poem that “Dear Olives” creator provided as a basis for an animated love letter from the farmer to the olives. Dear Olives is an ultra-premium extra virgin olive oil product, with a distinctive identity. As a motion designer, I couldn’t be happier to take on such a challenge, as I’ve sensed early on, an opportunity to tell an engaging visual story using an illustrative style similar to the illustrations decorating the products bottle and packaging. By trying to reproduce as close as possible the same style of illustration on the bottle within the animation, I wanted to ensure that whenever a consumer sees the illustrations on the bottle will remember the animated story of the olives with all the emotions that it involves.

Early Exploration

At first, the client asked for an animation based on the words of the poem: A Kinetic typography animation style, that puts emphasis on some of the important parts in the poem, narrated from the point of view of the farmer. But after listening to the poem, my brain was instantly brimming with ideas and visuals. I immediately felt that the words, the meanings hidden between the lines, the emotions expressed in the tone, were begging to be expressed with a visual story in an illustrative, cinematic way. And I saw an opportunity to try a new style, a new process that I’ve never tried before. I’m not going to lie, I’ve had a lot of doubts, since I’m mainly an animator and I’ve had a very little experience in illustration, and no one in my team had experience in the style that I was aiming for. But I felt that I needed to seize the opportunity and see what I’m capable of. So, I started right away, storyboarding the idea that I got.

A Hit And Miss

The client liked the idea of telling a visual story, with the style of the illustrations already on the packaging. And they agreed that a kinetic typography approach might be a disservice to the depth of the poem. But, they wanted to focus the story mainly on the olives and make sure that the verses of the poem be more integrated into the visual and not treated as an afterthought.

A Simplified approach

Based on the feedback of the client, I changed my approach in the second proposition, and I opted for a minimalistic, more iconic approach. My main focus was to treat the lettering as integral component of the visuals, and creating a more symbolic and geometric interpretation of the meanings, that will let the verses breath and reflect the journey of the olives in a more abstract, less literal way compared to the initial approach. After presenting these boards to the client, they felt that we lost the charm of the cinematic quality of the first approach and they didn't like the abstract approach, since it strayed away from the style of the illustration's style residing on the product. So, I got back again to the drafting table, with a puzzling question on my mind: How can I solve these problems without creating a competition for attention between the visuals and the lettering?

Some of the requests by the client, is to humanize the olives, through their story and to make the viewer fall in love with them.

That's how I got the idea to tell the story of a small olive from birth, to being withing family, an abrupt journey to the unknown, metamorphose, then living on through their transformation into the golden virgin oil. I wanted also to create a symbiotic relationship between them and the elements of nature through their journey.

STYLE I took inspiration from the roman and the Persian ancient pottery that contains paintings that tells stories of adventures and glory. I envisioned to set the start and the finish of our visual story on the label of the bottle, making it the canvas, where our story unveils.

By trying to reproduce as close as possible the same style of illustration on the bottle within the animation, I wanted to ensure that whenever a costumer sees the illustrations on the bottle and reads the poem on the bottles, will remember the animated story of the olives with all the emotions that it involves. My intent by that was to transcend the decorative function of the illustrations and give them meaning by turning them into a tool that visualizes the glorious tale of our protagonists: The olives family. Also, I found out that merging all the sentences of the poem with the illustrated animation will disturb the focus on the main story. So, I opted to show a selection of the sentences from the poem and alternate between them and between the illustrated shots all along the animation in a separate, harmonious way.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Dan Rice • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Titles, Motion Design, 3d

Title Design

A time-lapse of the near future for Amazon.

Client: Amazon
Studio: Breeder
My role: Creative Director, 2D animation, compositing and 3D
Team: five of us, all working remotely at the start of the 2020 lockdowns

The Expanse titles start high above Earth, zoom in, then pull out further and further through the solar system, an impressionistic time-lapse of humanity spreading outward.

The sequence changes as the story does, and in Season 5 it changed a lot.

There were five of us: me as Creative Director, Steph Walsh as Producer, Ryan McShane as Art Director, Joel Sankey as 3D Lead, and Jacob Stanley helping on 3D.

We kicked off a week or two after the Breeder studio went into lockdown and we were told to take our laptops home. It was surreal talking to the showrunner, Naren Shankar, from the basement of the place I was living in at the time, a very big, official project in a very unofficial setting.

The live-action plates were shot locally at the start of the 2020 lockdown, then built up into the finished shots. Because of the strict lockdowns we weren't able to hire crews to film the plates.

For shot 5 I packed up my camera kit, enlisted the help of my now wife and rolled out to a local beach to scout the location. These initial tests felt a bit too end of the world for The Expanse team, so I went back out and shot another plate at a calmer, classic bay. It was a lesson in doing a lot with a little.

Shot 5 follows a lonely figure walking towards a beach as ships launch in the distance and fly towards the moon. It's very blue and cool, with the classic Expanse flame trails behind the ships.

On top of the beach plate, I added the distant cities, the ships flying up and the moon, then did a colour pass. I stood in as the figure myself, then cleaned up the plate, shrank my silhouette down to the size the shot needed and composited it in.

Showrunner Naren Shankar asked to use the woman from the tests instead of my silhouette, so my wife, who had only come along to help me scout, ended up in the final titles.

There's also an Easter egg: a little fish jumps out of the water. I could easily have left it out, but I picked the section of the shot so it stays in. The splash down lands perfectly with the edit. It works to add life to the scene. In later episodes, once the shot changes, the ocean is noticeably lifeless.

My first take on shot 5 was a lot closer, with a large figure in frame and the background elements nearer too. Naren saw it and wanted to go back to the wide feel that previous seasons had set up.

In the final, the figure is tiny, right at the bottom of the shot, instead of closer to the centre of the frame.

The Expanse titles evolve every season, and they change within a season too, to follow what's happening in the story. In Season 5, nearly every episode got its own update.

Shot 5 is one example: it opens on a lone figure watching ships fly to the moon, later an asteroid heads for Earth, once it makes landfall the landscape is red and destroyed.

The asteroids creep closer to Earth with each episode, and more planets appear as ships fly to the further reaches of space as the story progresses. We also followed Marcos Inaros' stealth ships closing in on our heroes.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Nuno Leites • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 2d

MOTION BRANDING

Famel is a Portuguese brand focused on the motorbike industry since the 50s. The brand has become a national symbol and, even today, its motorbikes remain in the garage of many people.

The company declared bankruptcy in 2002 but, recently, was object of a total revitalization with the intention of rebuilding the whole brand and focus on the electric mobility. For this new electric era, Famel needed a rebranding that would communicate the new values and mission without erasing the rich past and legacy.

I had the privilege of being invited to take part of this creative process and think about how to elevate the brand with motion applied to the logo, social media assets, video transitions and a short motion film revealing the new brand identity.

The most important part of applying motion to the branding was to conceive small but distinctive behaviors that would emphasize freedom, speed, innovation and electric sustainable power.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Dan Rice • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, Titles, Mixed Media

Opening Sequence

Decades of Halfbrick characters. One very crowded screen. The opening sequence for Halfbrick+ mixes 2D, 3D, frame by frame, puppet animation, pixel art and simulated practical effects, like paper tearing.

“Goal: Make a memorable launch experience so awesome that people won't skip it even if they've seen it before.”

— Halfbrick Marketing Team

Halfbrick invited me to pitch on the opening sequence for their subscription platform, Halfbrick+.

Like most people, I was blown away the first time I played Fruit Ninja, so the chance to help shape how players are welcomed to the platform was a thrill.

The brief from Halfbrick’s marketing team was for an opening sequence that's exciting and celebrates everything Halfbrick. The answer was to bring nearly every character from their games together in one sequence.

There is no one art style that defines a Halfbrick game. Characters from decades of games each come from their own world, with their own look.

My pitch was a bricollage: a mixed media sequence that brings every character into the same space without losing what makes each one distinctive. We took the worlds and interfaces players already know and remixed them.

It also let us mix animation styles freely, from cel and puppet animation to UI animation and 3D.

“BRICOLAGE (bree-koh-LAHZH)”

— NOUN: CONSTRUCTION (AS OF A SCULPTURE OR A STRUCTURE OF IDEAS) ACHIEVED BY USING WHATEVER COMES TO HAND.

THE PITCH

Initial Design

Nobody knows the Halfbrick brand better than the people behind it, so I brought them into the process.

Drawing on my work with startups, I ran workshops with the team. We began with a kickoff to pin down what they wanted the sequence to achieve and hear their first ideas. Then we ran a brainstorm to dig up scenes, scenarios, funny moments and Easter eggs that felt true to the characters and games.

One of my favourites which made the final cut: Sensei riding on top of Colossotron like Paul Atreides on a sandworm.

I developed the visual story structure with Halfbrick’s Brendan Deboy. Starting from the rough boards and animatic from my pitch, plus the updated narrative from the workshops, Brendan sketched the first pass of the boards. From there we went back and forth, refining the sequence until the story structure was locked.

PRE-PRODUCTION

Boardimatic

PRE-PRODUCTION

Styleframes

PRODUCTION

Character Animation

I wanted the opener to feel like a Saturday-morning cartoon intro crossed with a roller-coaster ride: fast, loud and impossible to skip.

I directed the piece, and I also cut it, composited it and handled the 3D. Each artist’s shots went straight into the timeline as they landed, so I could judge them in context, tighten the timing frame by frame and send back precise notes. With one person carrying every shot through to the final composite, the sequence holds together from first frame to last.

Transitions turn a string of scenes into a ride. Every cut hands its energy to the next shot, using match cuts, colour matches, movement matches and cuts on action.

Barry rips his shirt, and the tear splits the screen like paper to reveal Colossotron. Sensei lifts an apple, we crash zoom into it, and the red colour matches to a button. A bear flies at the camera, we enter its mouth, and a fish swimming past match cuts to a bomb.

The edit only stops once. Dan the Man’s fly kick cracks the screen to white, then the rapid-fire ending kicks in.

Halfbrick+ is built for mobile, so the opener had to hold up on everything from small phones to tablets. I kept the most important element of every shot in the centre of frame. It gives the sequence its ride-like momentum, and it means nothing gets cropped on any screen.

We delivered five versions, set up so the Halfbrick team can create any other format they need without coming back to me.
